## Summary

Eisman acknowledges his earlier 4.5% Treasury threshold was wrong, then discusses a 5% threshold, FICO competition and AI leadership's safety rhetoric. He sees a regulatory-moat motive but offers no evidence proving intent. His unqualified tax-deferral suggestion via shorting appreciated shares is contradicted by constructive-sale rules and is partly corrected in the following week. Defensive portfolio suggestions and insurance pricing observations are mechanisms, not verified excess-return forecasts.

Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.

<a id="youtube-Q1jSJG1iBL8-c018"></a>
### 018. An investor can reduce appreciated Nvidia exposure by shorting the same shares and later removing the short instead of selling and triggering gains tax.

**Wrong** | Steve Eisman | analytical principle | supporting

[Source at 21:06-22:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q1jSJG1iBL8&t=1266s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The unqualified tax-deferral implication omits the constructive-sale rule: shorting the same appreciated stock normally realizes the gain. A narrowly conditioned exception exists and is discussed in the next wrap.

Assessment test: Apply IRC constructive-sale rules, including all closed-transaction exception conditions.

- [Publication 550 (2025): Constructive Sales](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p550) (2025 tax-year edition, inspected 2026-11-10): Shorting the same appreciated stock generally creates a taxable constructive sale. The closed-transaction exception requires close by 30 days after tax-year-end, 60 days continued ownership and no reduction of risk during those 60 days.
